subject_line: Family anecdotes turned poems in Everybody Is a Bridge
email_body:
Dear Anton,

I was drawn to the way Everybody Is a Bridge gathers poems, prose poems, notes and fragments around your own youth and later years as a white South African, with relatives and friends turning up as small pieces of anecdotal history. I'd like to ask how you decided which memories stayed as fragments and which grew into full poems.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait is developed through a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: Everybody Is a Bridge (2023) mixes poems/prose poems/fragments drawing on his youth as a white South African, relatives as anecdotal history (African Books Collective/Clarke's listing); HoD Literary Studies in English, Rhodes. Email seen in search result (Rhodes 2026 course guides/staff page).

book_title: Ice Cream Headache in My Bone
subject_line: Memory and the images in Ice Cream Headache in My Bone
email_body:
Dear Phillippa,

Reading about Ice Cream Headache in My Bone, your third collection, I was struck by how reviewers described its images drawn from memory as both euphoric and horrifying at once, and how far it travels from The Everyday Wife, which won the 2011 South African Literary Award for poetry. I'd love to ask how holding those two extremes in a single image works for you, on the page and in performance.

hook_note: Ice Cream Headache in My Bone (Modjaji, 2017), third collection, images from memory 'euphoric and horrifying' per listings; The Everyday Wife won 2011 SALA. Honours convenor, Wits Creative Writing. Email seen in search result (Wits staff page).

subject_line: Archéologie des Trous before An Archaeology of Holes
email_body:
Dear Stacy,

I was intrigued that An Archaeology of Holes reached readers first in French, as Archéologie des Trous in Paris in 2022, before the English edition followed in 2023, several years after the stories of Because the Night. I'd like to ask what it was like to see these pieces live in translation before they appeared in the language you wrote them in, and whether that changed how you read them.

subject_line: Walking Johannesburg under lockdown in The Near North
email_body:
Dear Ivan,

The Near North caught my attention for its premise: a writer walking the streets of Johannesburg through the city's different states of lockdown, a city you have been mapping on the page for decades. With a UK and Irish edition now on its way, I'd like to ask what those restricted walks let you notice about familiar streets that ordinary times had hidden.

subject_line: The body in the sequence of Fall Risk
email_body:
Dear Kobus,

I came across Fall Risk, launched at Amazwi in Makhanda in 2025, and its description as a sequence of poems on disability, ill health and ageing. Having read about A Book of Rooms and your 2025 inaugural lecture at UWC on how to teach people to write poetry, I'd like to ask why this material wanted to be a single sequence rather than separate poems, and how that choice shaped the writing.

subject_line: From Small Moving Parts to Otherwise Occupied
email_body:
Dear Sally-Ann,

I noticed that your writing has moved between forms: your debut novel Small Moving Parts won the Herman Charles Bosman Prize in 2010, and your 2019 poetry collection Otherwise Occupied was nominated for a South African Literary Award. I'd like to ask how you know whether a piece of material belongs to fiction or to poetry, and whether teaching creative writing at Stellenbosch has changed the way you make that call.
